questions.question: The scenario starts with `escape("<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>")`. Which branch of `escape` handles this value, what helper does it call, and what exact string does the resulting Markup hold?
questions.key: Because `type(s) is str` is true (line 39), the fast path is taken: `escape` skips the `__html__` check and the `str(s)` conversion entirely and returns `Markup(_escape_inner(s))`. `_escape_inner` replaces the five characters `& > < ' "`, so the result is `Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')` — the parentheses, semicolons and dots are untouched. The return type is exactly `Markup`.
questions.check:
import sys
try:
    import markupsafe
except ImportError:
    sys.path.insert(0, 'src')
    import markupsafe
r = markupsafe.escape('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')
assert type(r) is markupsafe.Markup
assert str(r) == '<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>'

questions.question: The scenario asserts `escape(safe_comment) == safe_comment` where `safe_comment` is a `Markup`. Which branch does `escape` take, and how many times is `__html__()` invoked during that single `escape()` call?
questions.key: `type(s) is str` is False (the type is `Markup`, a str subclass), so the `hasattr(s, "__html__")` branch is taken and `Markup(s.__html__())` is returned; `_escape_inner` is never called, so the text is unchanged (escaping is idempotent). `__html__()` runs twice: once in `escape` (line 43) and once again inside `Markup.__new__`, which also checks `hasattr(object, "__html__")` and replaces the object with its result (lines 125-126). This matches trace lines 11-16.
questions.check:
import sys
try:
    import markupsafe
except ImportError:
    sys.path.insert(0, 'src')
    import markupsafe
calls = []
class M(markupsafe.Markup):
    def __html__(self):
        calls.append(1)
        return self
m = M('<script>')
r = markupsafe.escape(m)
assert len(calls) == 2, calls
assert str(r) == '<script>'
assert type(r) is markupsafe.Markup

questions.question: When `template.format(user=user, comment=safe_comment)` reaches the `{user:link}` field, what does `EscapeFormatter.format_field` do with the `User` instance, and why is the returned `<a href=...>` markup not escaped again before being spliced into the result?
questions.key: `format_field` sees `hasattr(value, "__html_format__")` first (line 340), so it calls `user.__html_format__('link')`, which returns `Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"')`. The result is then passed through `str(self.escape(rv))` (line 354); since `rv` is a `Markup`, `escape` takes the `__html__` branch and returns it unchanged, so the tags survive while the name stays escaped. `User.__format__`/`str.format` default formatting is never used.

questions.question: The `{comment}` field of the template receives `safe_comment`, a `Markup`. Which branch of `EscapeFormatter.format_field` handles it, and what would happen instead if the template had been written `{comment:>40}`?
questions.key: `Markup` itself defines `__html_format__`, so the first branch is taken: `Markup.__html_format__('')` is called; since `format_spec` is empty it simply returns `self`, and `str(self.escape(rv))` leaves the already-escaped text alone, giving `<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>`. With `{comment:>40}` the spec is non-empty, so `Markup.__html_format__` raises `ValueError("Unsupported format specification for Markup.")` — Markup does not support format specs at all.

questions.question: Inside `User.__html__`, `Markup('{0}').format(self.name)` is evaluated with `name = 'Alice "The Great"'`. What exactly does the formatted value contain, and why are the quotes in `class="user"` not escaped?
questions.key: Only the substituted field goes through `EscapeFormatter.format_field`: `name` is a plain `str` with no `__html_format__`/`__html__`, so it falls to `super().format_field(...)` and is then escaped, becoming `Alice "The <b>Great</b>"` (double quote → `"`). questions.question: The scenario also calls `escape(user)` directly on the `User` object (which defines both `__html__` and `__html_format__`). Which of the two methods does `escape` use, and what is the result?
questions.key: `escape` never looks at `__html_format__`; after `type(s) is str` fails it checks `hasattr(s, "__html__")` and returns `Markup(s.__html__())`, trusting that output as already safe. So the result is `Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"')` — the span tag is preserved unescaped while the name was escaped by `User.__html__` itself. `__html_format__` is only consulted by `EscapeFormatter.format_field`.

questions.question: `escape` tests `type(s) is str` rather than `isinstance(s, str)`. What does this buy, and how are str subclasses and proxy objects handled as a result?
questions.key: The identity check is the fast path for the most common case — a plain `str` is sent straight to `_escape_inner` without the `__html__` lookup or a `str()` conversion. `type(s)` is used instead of `s.__class__` because a proxy object may report the `__class__` of the value it proxies (fix from 3.0.1); such a proxy therefore falls through to the generic path and is escaped via `str(s)`. Any `str` subclass likewise skips the fast path: `Markup` (and anything else with `__html__`) is returned unescaped through `Markup(s.__html__())`, while a subclass without `__html__` is escaped after `str(s)` — which is why `_escape_inner(str(s))` must tolerate `str(s)` returning a subclass instance (3.0.2 fix).

questions.question: What does `Markup(object, encoding=None, errors="strict")` do with each argument, and what is the trap when passing bytes without an encoding?
questions.key: `Markup.__new__` first checks `hasattr(object, "__html__")` and, if present, replaces `object` with `object.__html__()` — so wrapping an HTML-aware object marks its HTML output safe. If `encoding is None` it calls `str.__new__(cls, object)`, i.e. plain `str()` conversion with no escaping at all; otherwise it calls `str.__new__(cls, object, encoding, errors)` to decode a bytes-like object. The trap: `Markup(b"<b>hi")` with no encoding yields the repr-ish text `b'<b>hi'` rather than decoded text; you must pass e.g. `Markup(b"<b>hi", "utf-8")`. More generally the constructor never escapes — anything passed in is declared safe, so passing untrusted data here defeats the protection.

questions.question: How do `escape` and `escape_silent` differ for `None`, and what does `soft_str` guarantee?
questions.key: `escape(None)` has no fast path and no `__html__`, so it escapes `str(None)` and returns `Markup('None')` — the literal word "None" appears in output. `escape_silent` returns an empty `Markup()` for `None` (its only special case) and otherwise just delegates to `escape`; it is meant for optional values. `soft_str` returns the object unchanged if it is already a `str` instance — preserving a `Markup` so it will not be escaped a second time — and otherwise returns `str(s)`; note the isinstance check means any str subclass is passed through as-is.
questions.check:
import sys
try:
    import markupsafe
except ImportError:
    sys.path.insert(0, 'src')
    import markupsafe
from markupsafe import escape, escape_silent, soft_str, Markup
assert str(escape(None)) == 'None'
assert str(escape_silent(None)) == '' and type(escape_silent(None)) is Markup
assert str(escape_silent('<foo>')) == '<foo>'
m = Markup('<b>')
assert soft_str(m) is m and type(soft_str(15)) is str

questions.question: How does the package decide between the C speedups and the pure-Python implementation, and what is guaranteed to be identical between them?
questions.key: `src/markupsafe/__init__.py` does `try: from ._speedups import _escape_inner / except ImportError: from ._native import _escape_inner` at import time — a single module-level binding, chosen once; if the C extension was not built (setup.py falls back to a pure-Python build on compile failure or on PyPy/Jython/GraalVM) the native version is used transparently. Both implement the same contract: replace exactly `&`→`&`, `>`→`>`, `<`→`<`, `'`→`'`, `"`→`"` and nothing else, returning the text unchanged when no such characters occur (the C version then just increfs and returns the input object). Everything else — `Markup`, `escape`'s `__html__` handling — is pure Python either way.
questions.check:
import sys
try:
    import markupsafe
except ImportError:
    sys.path.insert(0, 'src')
    import markupsafe
from markupsafe._native import _escape_inner as native
assert native("&><'\"") == '&><'"'
assert str(markupsafe.escape("&><'\"")) == native("&><'\"")
assert native('plain text') == 'plain text'

questions.question: What exactly does `Markup.striptags` promise, and in which situations does it leave markup-looking text behind?
questions.key: It removes HTML comments first (repeatedly deleting from `<!--` through the next `-->`), then removes tags (from each `<` through the next `>`), then collapses all whitespace runs to single spaces via `" ".join(value.split())`, and finally returns `unescape()`d text. Comments are handled before tags so a comment containing a tag does not end early. If a `<!--` has no matching `-->`, or a `<` has no matching `>`, the loop breaks and that remainder is kept verbatim (e.g. `Markup("a<b").striptags() == "a<b"`). The return value is a plain `str` with entities decoded, so it is *not* safe markup: re-inserting it into HTML without escaping can reintroduce tags such as `<script>`.
questions.check: import sys try: import markupsafe except ImportError: sys.path.insert(0, 'src') import markupsafe from markupsafe import Markup assert Markup('xy&z').striptags() == 'xy&z' assert Markup('aAbout').striptags() == 'Main \u00bb About' assert type(Markup('x').striptags()) is str

questions.question: Describe the three-step dispatch in `EscapeFormatter.format_field` and the error it raises for a class that defines `__html__` but not `__html_format__`.
questions.key: For each substituted field: (1) if the value has `__html_format__`, it is called with the format spec and its return value used; (2) otherwise, if the value has `__html__`, it is called — but if a non-empty `format_spec` was given, a `ValueError` is raised with the message "Format specifier {spec} given, but {type(value)} does not define __html_format__. A class that defines __html__ must define __html_format__ to work with format specifiers."; (3) otherwise Python's default `string.Formatter.format_field` is used with `str(format_spec)`. In every case the result is finally passed through `str(self.escape(rv))`, so plain values get escaped while `Markup`/`__html__` output passes through unchanged.

dropped.question: Markup overrides many `str` methods. Which of them escape their arguments and which deliberately do not, and what is the stated rationale for the ones that don't?
dropped.key: Escaping overrides: `join` escapes every item of the iterable; `replace` escapes only its `new` argument (not `old`); `ljust`, `rjust`, and `center` escape `fillchar`; `__add__`/`__radd__` escape the other operand; `__mod__` escapes each interpolated value; `format`/`format_map` escape fields via `EscapeFormatter`. Non-escaping overrides merely re-wrap the result in the class: `strip`, `lstrip`, `rstrip`, `removeprefix`, `removesuffix`, `partition`, `rpartition`, plus `split`/`rsplit`/`splitlines`, `__getitem__`, `capitalize`, `title`, `lower`, `upper`, `swapcase`, `casefold`, `translate`, `expandtabs`, `zfill`, `__mul__`/`__rmul__`. Since 3.0.0 those search-like methods do not escape their argument because they are conceptually linked to `in`, `find`, `index`, which never escaped their arguments either.
